blocks.text: The sweep is a discrete derivative of the active-count function. Before s, the interval contributes zero; at s it becomes active, so add one; at e it stops contributing under [s, e), so subtract one. Prefix-summing all ordered event deltas reconstructs the number of active intervals between event coordinates. Weighted intervals replace one with the demand weight, but the signs remain the same. The endpoint contract still controls equal-coordinate ordering and whether the end transition occurs before or after starts at the same point.

messages.text: This reverses acquisition and release, producing negative active counts before intervals begin.
The end must remove the interval's contribution. Adding at both endpoints makes active demand grow permanently.

blocks.text: Equal-coordinate ordering is part of the sweep contract whenever intermediate states matter. With active = 1 before t, processing start first yields 2 and may record a false overlap; processing end first yields 0 then 1, matching legal reuse. The net delta after both events is zero, which is why an implementation that only examines final grouped state can appear correct on some outputs. It must nevertheless prove that no lost intermediate state affects the requested result. Closed intervals require the opposite tie because both intervals include t.

blocks.text: Closed endpoint semantics change event order, not merely the comparison syntax. If one interval ends at t and another begins at t, both sets contain t. Applying the start increment first exposes the concurrent state; applying the end first erases it. Grouping to a net zero delta also erases the peak. This matters for point-sensitive capacity or geometric intersection. If the application intentionally ignores measure-zero intersections, it must declare that alternate policy rather than silently using the half-open tie.

blocks.text: The two correct statements connect domain semantics to event order. Half-open intervals release before acquisition, so an ending delta precedes a starting delta when intermediate counts are inspected. Arbitrary ordering can create a transient extra active interval. Aggregating to a net delta can be safe for a narrowly defined result, but it discards within-coordinate transitions such as active reaching zero and reopening. Therefore grouping is an optimization that needs a proof for the exact answer contract, not a substitute for specifying ties.

blocks.text: Consider [0, 100) and [50, 60). End sorting processes the shorter interval first even though the long interval's start at 0 is the earliest event. Emitting both events of each interval in that order would process time 50 before time 0 and corrupt the prefix state. The correct procedure materializes or otherwise merges all endpoint events by coordinate. End sorting can still be useful inside a different algorithm, such as a heap of active releases or an earliest-finish greedy proof, but it is not the sweep's chronological axis.

messages.text: Distinct end times do not fix the problem: [50, 60) is end-sorted before [0, 100), even though time 0 must be processed before time 50.
A sweep does the opposite: it globally orders every endpoint, so events from different intervals may interleave. Keeping each pair adjacent would corrupt chronology.

feedback.reason: A sweep needs a single chronological order over every start and end event, which cannot be inferred from interval end order alone.

options.text: An early start can belong to an interval with a late end, so interval-end order does not globally order all event coordinates.
End order fails only for equal ends; a stable tie-break otherwise makes it chronological.

blocks.text: During [5.2, 5.8), both short intervals contribute, so the event prefix reaches two. The long-interval case has only one +1 before its -1, so the prefix never exceeds one. A sweep makes the distinction explicit: peak is the maximum prefix sum, not the width between events. Length may matter for union measure or total resource-hours, but it cannot replace active-count accumulation. This counterexample prevents a duration-based ranking from being mistaken for overlap intensity.

blocks.text: Creating events costs O(n), sorting 2n events costs O(2n log(2n)) = O(n log n), and the final scan costs O(n). The stored event list contains O(n) records. If coordinates come from a small bounded integer universe U, a counting or difference-array approach may achieve O(n + U) time and O(U) space, but that is a different precondition and representation. Sorting intervals by end does not reduce the need for chronological event order. The cost derivation follows the number of events and the sorting model, not interval lengths.

feedback.reason: There are 2n events; comparison sorting dominates at O(n log n), and the explicit event list uses O(n) space.

blocks.text: On a discrete integer line, [l, r] contains l, l + 1, ..., r. The difference update +1 at l and -1 at r + 1 keeps the prefix active through r and removes it before the next integer. The conversion requires a safe successor; if r is the maximum representable value, adding one can overflow and the representation must change. This transfer reuses half-open sweep mechanics while preserving closed input meaning. It is not valid for continuous coordinates, where there is no unique next point after r.
